title: The Battle of Hastings
anachronisms_found: Player One is given a full Norman base kit — TOWN_CENTER, ARCHERY_RANGE, BARRACKS, BLACKSMITH, STABLE, MONASTERY — for a single-day field battle; the only structure the Normans actually raised near Hastings was the motte-and-bailey at their camp, which the engine's Castle or Watch Tower would have represented far better
Player Two (Saxons) likewise gets a TOWN_CENTER and MONASTERY on Senlac Hill; Harold's army arrived after a forced march from Stamford Bridge and had no such installations

2,560 TREE_OAK tiles bury the battlefield in dense woodland; Senlac was an open ridge with the Andredsweald forest only at the Saxon rear, and a forest-choked map makes the historically decisive cavalry manoeuvre and feigned retreats nonsensical
Ten SKIRMISHER for the Saxons overstates Anglo-Saxon missile capability — Harold's force was famously almost devoid of archers, which is precisely why the Norman bowmen mattered

'Norman Reinforcements ... Fresh Norman riders arrive from the coast' is invented; William received no reinforcements during the battle, and this misrepresents the day as a matter of attrition topped up from the ships

Harold is only a generic KING unit rather than a named hero; acceptable given no Harold exists in the engine, but a renamed hero-class unit was available and would have avoided the generic placeholder
strengths: WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR is the correct hero, actually present and commanding on 14 October 1066, and the player's defeat is keyed to his death — matching the real crisis when rumour of William's fall nearly broke the Norman line
Norman roster of KNIGHT + ARCHER + SPEARMAN correctly reflects the tripartite Norman host of cavalry, bowmen and infantry
Saxon roster of CHAMPION (axe-armed housecarls) plus mass SPEARMAN is a defensible engine rendering of the housecarl-and-fyrd shield wall
The scripted feigned-retreat sequence (Saxon Pursuit patrol trigger followed by Ambush Springs killing the isolated pursuers) reproduces the battle's genuinely decisive tactic
Victory requires slaying Harold, and the timed 'Nightfall' defeat with the shield wall still standing correctly encodes the real strategic logic: William had to win before dark or lose the campaign
justification: The combatants and the tactical arc are handled well: William is the right hero at the right battle, the Norman knight/archer/spearman mix against a champion-and-spearman shield wall is a sound engine translation, and the Saxon-pursuit-then-ambush triggers plus a nightfall time limit capture the two things a student should learn about Hastings. The material culture is where it slips — both armies are handed Town Centres, Barracks, Monasteries, a Blacksmith, Stable and Archery Range on what was a one-afternoon field, and 2,560 oak trees turn the open downland of Senlac into woodland that would forbid the very cavalry feints the text celebrates. The fabricated 'fresh Norman riders from the coast' reinforcement wave and ten Saxon Skirmishers also cut against the record, since William got no reinforcements and Harold had almost no archers.

title: Marco Polo on the Silk Road
anachronisms_found: EL_CID (Rodrigo Diaz, died 1099, Castile) placed as a caravan figure - wrong century and wrong region by nearly two hundred years; he is used to stand in for a 13th-century Venetian merchant
WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR (died 1087, Normandy/England) placed in the Polo caravan - an 11th-century Norman king has no business on the 1271 Silk Road
GENGHIS_KHAN placed as a GAIA object at the destination: Genghis died in 1227 and the Polos were received by his grandson Kublai Khan, whose hero unit exists in the editor and should have been used
KNIGHT x3 as caravan escort - heavy Latin-Christian shock cavalry crossing Persia and the Pamirs is implausible; camel riders or light cavalry escorts were available in the engine
SHEEP x6 standing in for the caravan's pack animals when TRADE_CART and camel units were available and far more representative of a Silk Road caravan
CASTLE/KEEP used to represent Shangdu, giving the Khan's summer palace generic European stone-fortress architecture; a Wonder or pagoda-style structure would have read better
strengths: Player Two's roster of cavalry archers, scout and light cavalry with YURT_A-D tents is an appropriate Central Asian steppe-raider material culture
Waypoint triggers stage the real route in order: Persian oasis, bandit country, the Pamir 'Roof of the World' pass, then Shangdu
Narration is factually sound - 1271 departure, Niccolo's earlier journey, Marco aged seventeen, three thousand miles, seventeen years of service to Kublai
Tents, pavilion, palm forest and rock formations give a credible desert-caravan staging area rather than a European battlefield
Loss condition tied to the survival of at least one pack animal correctly frames the caravan's cargo as the point of the expedition
justification: The narrative skeleton is genuinely good - the trigger chain walks the caravan from a Persian oasis through bandit ambushes and the Pamir passes to Shangdu, and the on-screen text gets the dates, Marco's age and his seventeen years of service right. But the placed content contradicts that text at every key point: the Polos are represented by El Cid and William the Conqueror, heroes dead for roughly two centuries and belonging to Spain and Normandy, while the Khan at Shangdu is Genghis rather than the Kublai the dialogue names, despite Kublai being available in the editor. Supporting choices compound the problem: European knights and crossbowmen as escorts, sheep instead of the available trade carts or camels as pack animals, and a European Castle standing in for the Khan's summer palace. A student would absorb the route and the framing correctly but leave with badly scrambled ideas about who was present.

GOLD_MINE x5, STONE_MINE x4, FORAGE_BUSH and livestock scattered on the map implies an economic base irrelevant to a one-afternoon battle
Scripted 'Fresh Norman riders arrive from the coast' reinforcement trigger is invented; William received no reinforcements during the battle and his whole army was already committed
strengths: WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR is the correct commander, present in person at Hastings, and is placed on the correct (Norman) side
Norman roster of KNIGHT + ARCHER + SPEARMAN correctly reflects the tripartite Norman host of cavalry, archers and foot
Anglo-Saxon side has zero cavalry, correctly representing an army that dismounted and fought on foot
CHAMPION x20 is a sensible engine proxy for axe-wielding housecarls, with SPEARMAN x20 standing in for the fyrd

justification: The scenario gets the belligerents and the leadership right: William the Conqueror commands a Norman force of knights, archers and spearmen against a cavalry-less Saxon host of Champions (housecarls) and Spearmen (fyrd), with Harold represented by a KING unit since the engine offers no Harold hero. The scripted arc is genuinely the battle's arc — feigned retreat, pursuing Saxons cut off and destroyed, archery attrition, and victory contingent on killing Harold before nightfall, with a nightfall defeat if the wall holds. The main faults are avoidable roster and building choices: ten Skirmishers for an army that had virtually no archers, a Town Center rather than the available Castle/tower for William's motte-and-bailey beachhead, Monasteries and gold/stone mines on a one-day battlefield, and a fabricated seaborne reinforcement wave. Nothing is out of century, so a student would leave with a broadly correct picture, mildly distorted by Saxon missile troops and phantom Norman reinforcements.

The invented 'fresh Norman riders from the coast' reinforcement is a small fabrication, but a student would still leave understanding the shield wall, the feint, and the significance of Harold's death.

The caravan itself is knights, crossbowmen and sheep when the engine offers trade carts and camels, and Shangdu is rendered as a European Castle and Keeps. title: The Battle of Tours
anachronisms_found: Player One's leader is WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR, a mounted Norman hero of 1066, standing in for Charles Martel — and mounted, which contradicts the scenario's own 'shield wall' of dismounted Frankish infantry
Player Two's leader is SALADIN (d. 1193, Ayyubid Egypt/Syria) representing the Umayyad emir Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi of 732 — over four centuries and a different dynasty removed

Player Three's leader is EL_CID (Castilian, d. 1099) representing Duke Odo of Aquitaine — wrong century and wrong polity, and an odd choice given El Cid fought Muslim and Christian rulers in Iberia, not Umayyad invaders in Gaul

KNIGHT units in the Umayyad roster: heavy Western-style lancers for an Arab-Berber raiding army; the engine offers Camel Rider, Light Cavalry and Cavalry Archer, which are used elsewhere in the roster, so the Knights were avoidable
PIKEMAN (a 14th-century weapon system) among the Frankish line where SPEARMAN/MILITIA/MAN_AT_ARMS would have sufficed

A full economic/military base for the Franks (TOWN_CENTER, BLACKSMITH, MONASTERY, ARCHERY_RANGE, two GUARD_TOWERS) on what the text describes as an improvised wooded ridge position — the Franks fought from a field formation, not a fortified settlement
strengths: 4,640 oak trees creating genuinely wooded high ground, matching the sources' emphasis on the Franks choosing broken, tree-covered terrain to blunt cavalry
Correct belligerents at the level of sides: Frankish infantry versus Umayyad cavalry, with Aquitanians as a distinct third force

Frankish roster is overwhelmingly infantry (Militia/Man-at-Arms/Champion/Spearman/Pikeman) while the Umayyad roster is entirely mounted (camels, cavalry archers, knights) — the correct tactical asymmetry of the battle

Scripted arc tracks the real narrative: successive cavalry charges against a static line, Odo's Aquitanians raiding the enemy camp, Abd al-Rahman's death in the melee, and the Umayyad army slipping away southward under cover of night
Direct quotation of the Mozarabic Chronicle's 'like a wall, immovable as a block of ice' as an ambient line
Victory conditions correctly hinge on killing Abd al-Rahman or forcing withdrawal rather than on conquest, and defeat on the line being overrun
justification: The scenario's text, terrain and event script are unusually faithful — a wooded ridge of 4,640 oaks, an all-infantry Frankish line against an all-cavalry Umayyad host, Odo's camp raid, Abd al-Rahman's death and the nocturnal withdrawal, capped by the Mozarabic Chronicle's 'wall of ice' quotation. That work is undermined by the three placed heroes: William the Conqueror (1066, and mounted) as Charles Martel, Saladin (d. 1193, Ayyubid) as Abd al-Rahman, and El Cid (d. 1099, Castile) as Duke Odo, none of whom belong to the eighth century or to this campaign. Secondary problems include Knights in the Umayyad line where Camel Riders and Cavalry Archers were already available, and a full Frankish town base (Town Center, Monastery, Blacksmith, Guard Towers) on a battlefield position. A student would grasp the tactics and outcome correctly but would leave with Saladin and William the Conqueror wrongly attached to 732.

title: The Battle of Tours
anachronisms_found: WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR used as Charles Martel - a Norman duke of 1066, over three centuries after Tours, and mounted rather than the dismounted Frankish infantry commander described in the text
SALADIN used as Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi - a 12th-century Ayyubid sultan, ~450 years too late, and Kurdish/Egyptian rather than Umayyad Andalusian
EL_CID used as Duke Odo of Aquitaine - an 11th-century Castilian, and a Christian Spaniard standing in for a Frankish/Aquitanian duke
KNIGHT x6 in the Umayyad army - the heavy mailed European knight is a High Medieval type and the wrong armament for 732 Arab-Berber horse; camel riders and cavalry archers alone would have served
PIKEMAN x4 in the Frankish line - pike formations and the halberd-era polearm postdate 732 by six centuries; MILITIA/SPEARMAN alone would have been period-plausible
GUARD_TOWER x2 and a full TOWN_CENTER in the Frankish position - fortified stone Castle-Age towers are out of place for an army encamped on a wooded ridge in 732
MONASTERY (Western late-medieval architecture set) in a battlefield encampment of 732
strengths: Correct belligerents: Frankish infantry versus Umayyad mounted force, with a third Aquitanian party under Odo
4,640 oak trees creating the genuinely wooded high ground between Tours and Poitiers, the terrain that historically blunted the cavalry charges
Frankish force is overwhelmingly infantry (militia/man-at-arms/champion/spearman) while the Umayyads are entirely mounted (camel riders, cavalry archers) - the correct tactical asymmetry
Scripted arc matches the sources: repeated cavalry charges against a static line, a raid on the Umayyad camp that draws horsemen away, the death of Abd al-Rahman, and a night withdrawal southward
Direct quotation of the Mozarabic Chronicle's 'like a wall, immovable as a block of ice' as an ambient line
justification: The strategic and narrative reconstruction is unusually good: a wooded ridge of 4,640 trees, an all-infantry Frankish line facing an all-mounted Umayyad force, timed charges, Odo's camp raid, and victory by slaying Abd al-Rahman or forcing withdrawal all track the historical account, capped by an accurate Mozarabic Chronicle quotation. The material culture undercuts it badly: all three commanders are heroes from the wrong century and wrong polity (William the Conqueror for Charles Martel, Saladin for Abd al-Rahman, El Cid for Duke Odo), and the Umayyad host fields six European KNIGHTs while the Franks carry PIKEMEN, both avoidable given camel riders, cavalry archers, and militia-line units were already placed. A student would absorb the correct tactical lesson about infantry holding wooded ground against cavalry but would attach it to a cast of 11th- and 12th-century figures who were nowhere near Poitiers in 732.

title: The Exile of El Cid
anachronisms_found: SALADIN placed as the enemy hero: Salah ad-Din was a Kurdish sultan of Egypt/Syria active c.1169-1193, a century later and 3,000 km away from Zaragoza's rivals or Valencia in 1081-1094. The dialogue calls the enemy 'Rival Raider Chief' and 'Governor of Valencia', so the hero unit directly contradicts the text; a generic Mameluke/Cavalry Archer or a scripted named King would have been available.

One enemy player serves as both the 'rival raiders' of the Ebro valley and the city of Valencia, so El Cid's actual opponents at Almenar/Tevar (Berenguer Ramon II of Barcelona and al-Hayib of Lerida, i.e. partly Christian Catalan forces) are collapsed into a single Saracen-style Muslim army.

CAMEL_RIDER x3 in an Iberian setting: camel cavalry was essentially absent from Andalusi and Taifa field armies; light javelin cavalry (jinetes) would be the regional norm, and the engine's Light Cavalry/Cavalry Archer units cover this better.

Al-Mu'tamin of Zaragoza, El Cid's actual employer and the pivot of the whole 1081-1086 period, exists only as a text line with no allied player or units, so the 'mercenary in Muslim service' premise is never enacted on the map.
strengths: EL_CID hero unit is the correct and period-appropriate protagonist, and the loss condition (El Cid's death = defeat) matches the retinue's dependence on him.
The chronology in the narration is accurate: banishment by Alfonso VI in 1081, service to al-Mu'tamin of Zaragoza against his rivals, and the capture of Valencia in 1094.
El Cid's roster of KNIGHT units plus Stable/Blacksmith reflects a small Castilian mounted retinue rather than an infantry host, which is historically apt.

The growth trigger (reinforcements and resources created after the raider camp falls, with narration about warriors flocking to his banner) captures the real mechanism by which the exile's mesnada expanded on plunder and reputation.
Valencia as a heavily walled coastal objective with a gate-breach beat, plus palm forest and coastal march, is regionally plausible terrain and architecture for the Levante.
justification: The narrative spine is genuinely El Cid's: 1081 exile by Alfonso VI, paid service to al-Mu'tamin of Zaragoza, then the 1094 seizure of Valencia in his own name, with El Cid's survival as the defeat condition. But the built content undercuts the text badly: the enemy commander is SALADIN, a late-12th-century Ayyubid sultan who never set foot in Iberia, standing in for both a Zaragozan rival chief and the governor of Valencia, and his force includes camel riders that no Taifa or Almoravid army in Valencia would have fielded. Al-Mu'tamin, the employer whose patronage defines the whole exile period, is given no player slot or units, so the mercenary relationship is only narrated, and the Catalan/Lerida opponents of Almenar and Tevar are replaced by a generic Muslim faction. A student would take away a correct outline of dates and outcomes but a confused impression that El Cid fought Saladin.

title: The Exile of El Cid
anachronisms_found: SALADIN placed as the enemy hero: Salah ad-Din (1137-1193) was a Kurdish sultan of Egypt and Syria, active a century after El Cid's exile and 3,000 km away. He was never in Iberia, and the engine offered avoidable alternatives (an unnamed Mameluke/Camel Rider, or a generic King in the Castle) to represent the taifa governor of Valencia (in reality Ibn Jahhaf/al-Qadir).

Nine CAVALRY_ARCHER as the core of the enemy army: Andalusi and taifa armies fought with light javelin cavalry (jinetes) and infantry archers, not the Turkic-style horse-archer mass; the engine's Light Cavalry/Skirmisher/Archer options would have been closer.
CAMEL_RIDER in an 11th-century Levantine-Spanish setting: camel cavalry belongs to North African/Near Eastern armies, marginal at best in taifa Valencia before the Almoravids.

The single enemy player is simultaneously the 'Rival Raider Chief' of the northern Ebro campaigns (in reality al-Hajib of Lleida plus Christian Aragon and Barcelona under Sancho Ramirez/Berenguer Ramon II) and the governor of Valencia, collapsing distinct belligerents into one Saladin-led faction.
strengths: EL_CID is the correct engine hero for Rodrigo Diaz de Vivar and his death is the correct defeat condition (the player's fortunes really did rest entirely on his person).
Dialogue correctly names Alfonso VI as the king who banished him in 1081 and al-Mu'tamin of Zaragoza as the Muslim patron he served as captain of armies - both historically exact.

The narrative arc (exile 1081 - mercenary service in the Ebro valley - restored reputation - independent conquest of Valencia in 1094) matches the real chronology, and the CHANGE_OWNERSHIP of Valencia to Player One correctly conveys that he took the city in his own name rather than Alfonso's.
Palm forest, coastal march 'south along the coast', and a walled city with Castle and gate are reasonable material choices for the Valencian littoral.
justification: The narrative scaffolding is genuinely well researched - Alfonso VI, al-Mu'tamin of Zaragoza, the 1081/1094 dates, and El Cid's survival as the win condition are all correct - but the placed content undercuts the text: the enemy is led by SALADIN, a 12th-century Ayyubid sultan who never set foot in Spain, fielding camel riders and nine cavalry archers rather than anything resembling a taifa or Aragonese force. The historically correct ally, al-Mu'tamin, exists only as blue text and is given no units or buildings, so the defining feature of the exile - a Christian knight commanding a Muslim king's army - never appears on the map. With 123 objects and four Knights as the 'retinue', a student would absorb the right chronology but a badly distorted picture of who El Cid actually fought and for whom.

title: The Battle of Tours
anachronisms_found: WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR stands in for Charles Martel — a Norman duke of 1066, over three centuries after 732, and mounted, contradicting the scenario's own 'Frankish infantry shield wall' premise

SALADIN represents Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi — a 12th-century Ayyubid sultan, 455 years out of period; the engine offers no 8th-century Umayyad hero, but a generic named unit or a less iconic hero would have been far less misleading
EL_CID as Duke Odo of Aquitaine — an 11th-century Castilian, and ironically a hero of the Reconquista placed on the Frankish/Aquitanian side

PIKEMAN x4 and CHAMPION x4 in the Frankish line: pike blocks and two-handed swordsmen are 14th–15th-century troop types; MILITIA/SPEARMAN alone would have represented Martel's spear-and-axe foot accurately

KNIGHT x6 for the Umayyad host — couched-lance heavy cavalry in Frankish-style plate iconography for an Arab-Berber raiding army; CAMEL_RIDER x7 in Poitou is likewise geographically improbable (the invaders' mounts were horses)
KNIGHT x3 and SCOUT_CAVALRY under Odo of Aquitaine reuse the same anachronistic heavy cavalry type
MONASTERY and GUARD_TOWER x2 in the Frankish battle camp — the Franks fought on an open wooded ridge, not from fortified stone works
strengths: Belligerents are correct: Frankish foot versus Umayyad cavalry, with Odo of Aquitaine as a genuinely present third force
Terrain is well chosen — 4,640 oak trees on a 120x120 map convincingly renders the wooded high ground between Tours and Poitiers that favoured the Frankish defence
Force composition ratio is right in spirit: the player's army is overwhelmingly foot, the enemy's is entirely mounted (camels, cavalry archers, knights) with a single villager as camp presence
The scripted arc is historically sound: repeated cavalry charges against an unbroken infantry line, a raid on the Umayyad camp, the death of Abd al-Rahman, and a nocturnal withdrawal southward
The quotation of the Mozarabic Chronicle's 'like a wall, immovable as a block of ice' is a genuine primary-source detail well deployed as ambient narration
justification: The scenario gets the shape of Tours right — a wooded ridge, an infantry-only defender, an all-cavalry attacker, the camp raid that historically broke Umayyad cohesion, Abd al-Rahman's death, and the night withdrawal — and the objective text names the real commanders. But every one of the three commanders on the field is an avoidably wrong-century hero unit: William the Conqueror (1066) plays Charles Martel, Saladin (1187) plays Abd al-Rahman, and El Cid plays Duke Odo, so a player sees Norman and Ayyubid figures fighting a 732 battle. The Frankish roster is further diluted by Pikemen and Champions when Militia and Spearmen were available and correct, and the loss triggers are miscoded to DECLARE_VICTORY, undercutting the otherwise sound outcome logic.

title: The Exile of El Cid
anachronisms_found: SALADIN placed as the enemy hero: Salah ad-Din was a Kurdish sultan of Egypt/Syria (1137-1193) who never set foot in Iberia and was born four decades after El Cid's death. He commands both the 'rival raider camp' near Zaragoza and Valencia, which is doubly wrong.

CAMEL_RIDER x3 for the Andalusi/Zaragozan side: taifa and even Almoravid field armies in eastern Iberia fought as light and heavy horse and foot; camelry is a Levantine/North African desert element, and the engine's Light Cavalry or Knight would have been a closer fit.
CAVALRY_ARCHER x9 as the enemy's main arm: mounted archery was not the signature of Iberian Muslim armies of the 1080s-90s; Andalusi forces relied on javelin-armed jinetes and foot archers.

The 'rivals raiding from the north' whom El Cid actually beat for al-Mu'tamin were the Christians of Aragon and Barcelona (and Muslim Lerida) - here they are rendered as a camel-and-Saladin Saracen camp, inverting the confessional line-up.
Al-Mu'tamin of Zaragoza, El Cid's actual employer, exists only as text; no allied player or unit represents Zaragoza, so the defining 'mercenary for a Muslim king' relationship is never on the map.
strengths: EL_CID hero is the correct, engine-available protagonist, and the 'El Cid must survive' defeat trigger reflects the retinue's total dependence on his person.
The chronological frame (1081 banishment by Alfonso VI to the 1094 capture of Valencia) is correct and the dialogue names the right figures: Alfonso VI, Al-Mu'tamin, and a Valencian governor.
Reward triggers that spawn new troops after the first victory model the historical growth of El Cid's mesnada as his prestige and plunder increased.

Valencia as a heavily walled coastal objective (53 stone walls, castle, guard towers, gate-breach trigger) with a march 'south along the coast' matches the geography and the fortified-city nature of the 1093-94 operation.
Palm forest and Mediterranean terrain are a reasonable evocation of the Valencian huerta rather than generic north-European woodland.
justification: The narrative spine - exile from Castile, paid service to al-Mu'tamin of Zaragoza against raiders, then the independent conquest of Valencia - is genuinely the arc of El Cid's exile, and the correct hero anchors the player's side with a fitting 'hero dies, you lose' rule. But the opposition is badly misidentified: SALADIN, a twelfth-century Ayyubid sultan of Egypt, leads both the Zaragozan rivals and Valencia, an entirely avoidable choice given the engine's generic and Iberian-appropriate alternatives, and his camel riders and nine cavalry archers import Levantine material culture into the Ebro valley and the Levante. Compounding this, the rivals El Cid actually crushed for al-Mu'tamin were Christian Aragonese and Catalans, so the scenario teaches a simple Christian-versus-Muslim frame that is the opposite of the taifa-era realpolitik it claims to depict, and al-Mu'tamin himself never appears as a player. A student would retain the correct dates and outcome but leave believing El Cid fought Saladin's camel troops.

title: The Road to Reims
anachronisms_found: The English garrison force is built around 9 CROSSBOWMEN with no LONGBOWMAN, even though the editor offers the Longbowman — the signature English missile arm of the 1420s is simply absent, and crossbows read as continental/Burgundian rather than English.
Narration calls Charles the 'boy-king'; the Dauphin was 26 in July 1429 and had been a functioning claimant for years — a factual mislabel, not an engine limit.

Troyes and Châlons are labelled purely 'England's' with an 'English Garrison Commander'; both towns were held by Anglo-BURGUNDIAN garrisons under Burgundian civic authority, and no Burgundian player or unit appears anywhere in the roster.
strengths: JOAN_OF_ARC is the correct hero for June–July 1429 and is on the correct (French) side.
The Dauphin is represented by a KING unit whose death triggers immediate defeat — a faithful mechanical expression of the fact that the whole march existed only to get Charles anointed.
Geography and sequence are right: Troyes, then Châlons, then Reims cathedral (a Gaia MONASTERY) eastward, matching the actual itinerary of the coronation march.
French roster (Knights, Man-at-Arms, Pikemen, Archers) is plausible for a mid-15th-century Valois field escort; Castle/stone wall/gate garrison towns are appropriate Champenois fortifications.
Closing text correctly names the outcome: anointing and coronation as Charles VII at Reims.
justification: The belligerents and the hero are right — Joan escorting a KING-unit Dauphin from Troyes through Châlons to Reims, with his death as the defeat condition, captures the real strategic logic. But the brief promises garrisons that 'can be fought or persuaded to surrender' while the triggers implement only DESTROY_OBJECT on two garrison commanders; the historically famous point about this march is that Troyes fell after brief siege and negotiation and Châlons opened its gates without a fight, so a scenario with no tribute/diplomacy path inverts the real character of the campaign. The opposition is also flattened into 'English' with Burgundy erased, and its missile core is nine Crossbowmen when the editor's Longbowman was available. A student would learn the correct route and purpose but come away thinking Champagne was stormed at swordpoint by a boy-king's army.

Both commanders are undifferentiated KING units, so a student learns the siege's shape but takes away a fifteenth-century crossbow-and-catapult impression of a 1529 gunpowder siege.

title: The Siege of Vienna
anachronisms_found: Both commanders are generic KING units. Niklas Graf Salm and Suleiman I are named only in dialogue; the engine offers numerous hero/named units and at minimum distinct unit types, so representing a German infantry captain and an Ottoman sultan with identical Kings is an avoidable flattening.

The garrison text promises 'Landsknechts! Arquebusiers!' but the placed roster is CHAMPION, PIKEMAN, CROSSBOWMAN, SKIRMISHER. Age of Empires II contains an actual Landsknecht unit and Hand Cannoneers/Arquebusier-equivalents; using crossbows and skirmishers for a 1529 defence understates the gunpowder infantry that actually held the walls.

No Janissaries in the Ottoman force, despite the Turkish unique unit being exactly the elite gunpowder infantry that led the assaults on the Carinthian Gate; instead the Sultan's army is built from CAMEL_RIDER, LIGHT_CAVALRY and CAVALRY_ARCHER.
Five Camel Riders as an assault force before Vienna is out of region; camels served the Ottoman train in the Balkans but camel cavalry was not a component of the 1529 storming parties.

A single BATTERING_RAM plus Suleiman's line 'Bring forth the ram!' misrepresents the siege: the Ottomans relied on mining and light field guns because their heavy artillery was bogged down on the Danube road, not on rams against Vienna's walls.
strengths: Correct belligerents: a Habsburg city garrison behind 123 stone wall segments, Castle and Keep versus an Ottoman camp of PAVILION and TENT sets with bonfire and standard.
Ottoman siege train includes BOMBARD_CANNON, MANGONEL and ONAGER, appropriate for 1529 artillery, and the camp is a separate encampment rather than a walled town.

The scripted arc is genuinely this siege: herald's surrender summons, sappers detected beneath the Carinthian bastion, mine detonation opening a breach, raiders pouring through, breach sealed, three escalating assaults, Ottoman council fretting over supplies, then October rains and the 14 October withdrawal.
Victory by survival-to-timer rather than by destroying the enemy correctly models a defensive siege whose outcome was Ottoman logistical failure, not battlefield annihilation.
ROMAN_RUINS on the map is a defensible touch for the site of Roman Vindobona, and the heavy oak cover suits the Vienna Woods approaches.
justification: The scenario gets the shape of 1529 right — the correct two sides, an Ottoman siege camp of tents and pavilions with bombard and mangonels, and a beat-by-beat sequence (surrender demand, mining under the Carinthian bastion, breach, three assaults, autumn rains, 14 October retreat) that matches the real course of the siege and its logistical outcome. The failure is in the placed rosters: the dialogue explicitly names Landsknechts and arquebusiers, yet the garrison consists of Champions, Pikemen, Crossbowmen and Skirmishers when the engine supplies both a Landsknecht unit and gunpowder handgunners, and the Ottomans field no Janissaries at all while including five Camel Riders. Both Salm and Suleiman are reduced to identical KING units, so the two commanders whose names carry the narrative are indistinguishable on the map. A student would leave with the correct story of the siege but a distinctly 14th-century picture of how it was fought.

The Mongol side is the one genuinely well-built element (yurts, palisade, cavalry archers, light cavalry), and the waypoint-to-Shangdu structure captures the journey's shape and correct endpoint. A student would leave believing Marco Polo fought his way into China against Kublai Khan's cavalry, which is the opposite of what happened.

title: The Battle of Hastings
anachronisms_found: 44 STONE_WALL segments, a GATE_NORTH_TO_SOUTH and 4 GUARD_TOWERs for the Anglo-Saxon player: Harold's army fought an open-field defensive action on the Senlac ridge with no fortifications whatsoever; the engine offered palisades or simply massed infantry, so a stone-walled fortress is an avoidable invention

TOWN_CENTER, MONASTERY, BLACKSMITH, STABLE and ARCHERY_RANGE for both sides turn a one-day field battle into a base-vs-base fight; neither army had installations at Senlac (William's only work was the prefab motte at Hastings, several miles off)
16 SKIRMISHERs in the Saxon roster: contemporary accounts (and the Bayeux Tapestry) show the English fielding essentially no missile troops at Hastings — that was the Norman advantage
Anglo-Saxon STABLE building implies mounted forces; Harold's housecarls dismounted to fight and the shield wall was entirely on foot
4174 TREE_OAK tiles render Senlac as dense forest; the ridge itself was open ground with the Andredsweald at the Saxon rear only
strengths: WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR is the correct commander for the Norman side and is correctly the player's hero whose death causes defeat
Harold is represented by a KING unit as the kill target — the engine has no Harold Godwinson hero, so this is a reasonable substitution, and 'Slay King Harold' matches the battle's decisive event

Norman roster of KNIGHT (mounted milites), ARCHER and MAN_AT_ARMS correctly reproduces the combined-arms cavalry/archer/infantry force, while the Saxon roster of CHAMPION (housecarls with axes) and SPEARMAN (fyrd levies) is an apt medieval-English match with no cavalry
Narrative beats track the real day: archers first, infantry probes, feigned retreats thinning the wall, and a final assault before nightfall on 14 October 1066
Dialogue correctly names Senlac Hill, housecarls, fyrd levies and the Saxon possession of the high ground
justification: The belligerents and heroes are right — William the Conqueror leads a knight/archer/man-at-arms Norman force against a cavalry-less Saxon army of Champions (housecarls) and Spearmen (fyrd) under a King standing in for Harold — and the scripted arc (archer volleys, probing infantry, feigned retreats thinning the wall, Harold's death collapsing the line before nightfall) is recognisably Hastings. The material culture is undermined by the Saxon player's 44 stone walls, gate and four guard towers plus Town Centres, monasteries and stables on both sides, which recast an open-ridge shield-wall battle as an assault on a fortified town; Harold held no fortification at Senlac and the engine's palisades or bare terrain were available alternatives. The 16 Saxon Skirmishers also invert the historical missile imbalance, which favoured the Normans. A student would grasp the commanders, the combined-arms tactic and the outcome, but would wrongly picture the English defending walls and towers, and the feigned retreat exists only in dialogue with no mechanic behind it.

title: The Battle of Hastings
anachronisms_found: 44 STONE_WALL segments, 4 GUARD_TOWERs and a gate for the Anglo-Saxon player: Harold's army fought from an unfortified ridge line at Senlac; there were no stone curtain walls or masonry towers on the field, and the trigger 'Close Gates' turns a field battle into a castle siege
STABLE built by the Anglo-Saxon player: Harold's housecarls and fyrd fought dismounted, and the absence of Saxon cavalry is one of the defining facts of the battle
TOWN_CENTER, BLACKSMITH, MONASTERY and MILL/HOUSE clusters for both sides imply settled economies on the battlefield; both armies were campaign forces with no such infrastructure at Hastings

SKIRMISHER x16 as the Saxon missile arm overstates Anglo-Saxon shooting capacity; contemporary accounts stress the Saxons had very few archers, which is why Norman arrows were reportedly returned so sparsely

4,174 oak trees on a 120x120 map produces dense forest, whereas the fighting took place on open slope and marshy ground between Senlac ridge and the Norman start line (the dialogue itself references a 'marshy field below the ridge')
strengths: Correct belligerents: Normans as the player, Anglo-Saxons as the enemy, with the WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR hero who genuinely commanded on 14 October 1066
Harold represented by a KING unit whose death triggers victory, matching the historical collapse of the shield wall after Harold's fall
Norman roster of KNIGHT, MAN_AT_ARMS and ARCHER is a fair engine rendering of the real combined-arms force of mounted milites, foot serjeants and bowmen
CHAMPION and SPEARMAN for the Saxon line is a defensible stand-in for axe-wielding housecarls and spear-armed fyrd
Scripted beats follow the real arc: archers first, infantry probe, feigned retreats drawing Saxons off the wall, thinning of the line, and a final assault before nightfall
Defeat condition tied to William's death reflects the genuine crisis when rumour of the Duke's death nearly broke the Norman army
Correct date, place name (Senlac Hill) and terminology (housecarls, fyrd levies) in the narration
justification: The scenario gets the belligerents and the leadership right: William the Conqueror leads the Norman player, the Saxon king is the kill-target, and the trigger sequence reproduces the real narrative of archery preparation, infantry probe, feigned retreat, and Harold's death ending the shield wall before nightfall. The material culture is where it slips: 44 stone wall segments, four guard towers and a closing gate convert an unfortified ridge into a walled fortress, and the Saxon STABLE contradicts the well-known fact that Harold's entire army fought on foot. Town centres, blacksmiths and monasteries on both sides are generic campaign filler rather than 1066 field armies, and 4,174 oak trees obscure the open slope the battle was actually fought over. A student would still leave with the correct outline of the battle, but with a false impression that Harold defended prepared stone works.

title: The Battle of Hastings
anachronisms_found: 44 STONE_WALL segments, a GATE_NORTH_TO_SOUTH and 4 GUARD_TOWERs for the Anglo-Saxon player: Harold's army fought behind a shield wall of men on an open ridge, with no masonry fortification at Senlac whatsoever. This turns a field battle into an assault on a walled fort and directly contradicts the scenario's own text about a shield wall.

Full economic/military base for the Normans (TOWN_CENTER, MILL, 3 HOUSES, BLACKSMITH, MONASTERY, STABLE, ARCHERY_RANGE, BARRACKS) — William's force landed at Pevensey weeks earlier and fought from a temporary camp; a settled town centre with houses and a mill is not present on the battlefield.

Saxon MONASTERY, TOWN_CENTER, STABLE and ARCHERY_RANGE placed on the ridge: Harold's army was a marching force with no such installations, and the stable implies mounted arms the Anglo-Saxons deliberately did not deploy (they dismounted to fight).

CHAMPION x25 for the housecarls — the engine offers TWO_HANDED_SWORDSMAN or the axe-armed alternatives that would read closer to 11th-century Danish-axe housecarls; Champion is a late-medieval plate-armoured profile.
ROMAN_RUINS as decoration on the Sussex battlefield is a mild out-of-place flourish for 1066 Senlac Hill.
4,174 TREE_OAK on a 120x120 map: Senlac was an open ridge with the Andredsweald forest behind the Saxon line, not near-total woodland, which also removes the open slope the cavalry charges required.

Anglo-Saxon roster of massed infantry (Champions as housecarls, Spearmen as fyrd levies, Skirmishers as javelin/sling throwers) with a KING standing in for Harold is a sensible use of the engine's catalogue, and no wrong-century named hero is used.
Norman roster of Knights (cavalry), Archers and Man-at-Arms correctly reflects the tripartite Norman combined-arms force described in the sources.

Objective logic mirrors the real outcome: killing Harold triggers victory and the shield wall's collapse, while William's death triggers defeat — echoing the real crisis when rumours of William's fall nearly routed the Normans.
Dialogue beats track the day's arc: archers first, then infantry to test the line, feigned retreats drawing Saxons off the wall, and a final decisive assault before nightfall on 14 October 1066.
justification: The belligerents and their leadership are right — William the Conqueror leads Normans of knights, archers and men-at-arms against a Saxon infantry mass with a King standing in for Harold — and the objective chain (break the wall, slay Harold, keep William alive) reproduces the real battle's decisive logic. The fatal material error is the Saxon position: 44 stone wall segments, a gate and four guard towers convert Senlac Hill's human shield wall into a fortified stronghold, flatly contradicting the scenario's own narration, and both sides are given town centres, monasteries, stables and a mill that had no existence on the 1066 battlefield. The celebrated feigned retreat is only spoken of in dialogue, never mechanised (the triggers merely PATROL enemy units), so the student learns the phrase without the tactic. Net result: correct cast and correct ending, but a battlefield that teaches a siege where a field battle occurred.

PAVILION_A / TENT_A for Odo's Aquitanians gives a Middle-Eastern nomad camp look to a Gallo-Roman Christian duchy

title: The Battle of Tours

title: The Exile of El Cid

37 CAMEL_RIDER units as the core of the Muslim army: taifa and even Almoravid forces in eastern Iberia fought as horse cavalry (jinetes/heavy horse) and infantry; camel cavalry en masse belongs to a North African/Levantine setting, and the engine's Cavalier/Light Cavalry/Cavalry Archer would have served.
18 TREE_PALM_FOREST tiles plus ROMAN_RUINS/TEMPLE_RUIN dressing give a Near-Eastern desert look rather than the Ebro valley and Levantine huerta of Zaragoza and Valencia.

Minaya Alvar Fanez speaks throughout the dialogue but no unit represents him; conversely no representation at all of Alfonso VI, al-Mutamin of Zaragoza, Berenguer Ramon II of Barcelona, or al-Qadir/Ibn Jahhaf of Valencia, the actual named parties of 1081-1094.

anachronisms_found: EL_CID placed as an English garrison commander: Rodrigo Diaz de Vivar died in 1099 and was a Castilian, not an Englishman - wrong century and wrong culture entirely

English garrisons armed only with CROSSBOWMAN when the engine provides the Longbowman for exactly this English force; crossbows were more a Burgundian/continental garrison weapon than the signature English archery of 1429
Troyes and Chalons are labelled purely 'sworn to King Henry' and staffed as English; both were in practice Anglo-Burgundian towns, and no Burgundian presence is represented in text or roster
strengths: JOAN_OF_ARC and a KING unit (the Dauphin) on the French side are the correct principals, and the defeat condition tied to the King's death matches the campaign's real stakes

The dual resolution for each town - [Troyes] Surrenders / [Troyes] Falls in Battle, same for Chalons - correctly models the historical pattern of towns opening their gates to the Maid rather than being stormed
A GAIA MONASTERY used as Reims cathedral with the arrival trigger and coronation text gives the correct terminal objective and outcome (Charles VII crowned)
ROMAN_RUINS near the objective is a nice touch for Reims, which retained Roman monuments such as the Porte de Mars
Heavy oak forest, forage bushes, deer and sheep, stone walls, keeps and guard towers are a plausible material setting for 15th-century Champagne
justification: The French side is well cast - Joan of Arc escorting a KING through hostile country, with the Dauphin's death as the defeat condition - and the fight-or-persuade branches at Troyes and Chalons genuinely reproduce the 1429 march's real dynamic of garrisons yielding to the Maid. But the English opposition is led by El Cid and William the Conqueror, an 11th-century Castilian and an 11th-century Norman, when the engine ships Sir John Fastolf from this very campaign; the English also field crossbowmen rather than the available Longbowman. The towns are also flattened into purely English holdings, erasing the Burgundian allegiance that actually made Troyes and Chalons hesitate. A student would leave with the right narrative arc but two badly misattributed enemy commanders and no sense of the Anglo-Burgundian alliance.

title: The Siege of Vienna
anachronisms_found: FREDERICK_BARBAROSSA placed as the Viennese commander: a 12th-century Hohenstaufen emperor standing in for Niklas Graf Salm, who is only named in text. Salm could have been represented by any generic hero/king unit rather than a 350-year-anachronistic named hero.
SALADIN placed as the Ottoman commander: an Ayyubid sultan of the 1180s substituting for Suleiman the Magnificent, wrong century and wrong dynasty entirely.

CAMEL_RIDER x5 in the Ottoman army: an Arab/Saracen unit; the 1529 besieging force's cavalry were sipahi and akinci, better served by Light Cavalry/Cavalry Archer (both of which are also present, making the camels gratuitous).

TREBUCHET and MANGONEL as the Ottoman siege train while the defenders hold the only BOMBARD_CANNONs: Suleiman's army was famous for gunpowder artillery (though it left its heaviest guns behind in the mud), and torsion/counterweight engines were obsolete by 1529.

Defender roster of KNIGHT, MAN_AT_ARMS, CROSSBOWMAN, SKIRMISHER, PIKEMAN: a 14th-century garrison. The text promises Landsknechts and Spanish arquebusiers; the engine offers Hand Cannoneers, Two-Handed Swordsmen/Champions and Halberdiers, so the pike-and-shot character of 1529 was achievable and was not attempted.
No janissaries represented despite the dialogue naming them; Hand Cannoneer or Janissary units were available in the engine.
strengths: The scripted beats follow the real arc: Ottoman arrival from Buda, detection of Ottoman sappers and a countermining sortie, three successive assaults concentrated on the Carinthian Gate, then autumn rains and supply failure prompting withdrawal.
The Carinthian Gate is correctly identified as the focus of the mining and the assaults, with a 'Gate Breached' trigger spawning attackers into the gap, mirroring the real breaches of 9-12 October.
Heavy STONE_WALL (268 segments), Keep, Castle and Guard Towers give a credible late-medieval Vienna enceinte rather than an open field battle, correctly framing this as a defensive siege.
The narration accurately attributes Ottoman failure to weather, short campaign season and logistics rather than to battlefield annihilation.
justification: The belligerents are broadly right (Ottoman besiegers vs a walled Vienna garrison) and the trigger sequence genuinely tracks 1529 - countermining the sappers, three assaults on the Carinthian Gate, autumn rains and withdrawal - but the placed content contradicts the text at almost every point. Frederick Barbarossa commands the defence in place of Salm and Saladin commands the Ottomans in place of Suleiman, two named heroes from the 1180s in a 1529 scenario; the promised Landsknechts and arquebusiers appear as Men-at-Arms, Crossbowmen and Skirmishers even though Champions and Hand Cannoneers were available, and the Ottomans field camel riders and a trebuchet while the defenders hold the only bombard cannon. The victory condition also falsifies the outcome by requiring Suleiman's death rather than modelling his intact withdrawal, so a student would leave with the impression that Vienna was saved by killing the Sultan.

title: Marco Polo on the Silk Road
anachronisms_found: RICHARD_THE_LIONHEART is the player's hero, evidently standing in for Marco Polo: Richard died in 1199, was an English crusader king, and had no connection to the Silk Road. Generic 'Merchant'/monk/king-type units or a renamed generic unit would have been far less jarring, so this was avoidable.

BERSERK as the bandit chief killed to recruit the caravan guards: a Scandinavian Viking unit with no place in 13th-century Central Asia; Tarkan, Mangudai, Camel Rider or Cavalry Archer were all available alternatives.

Five KNIGHTS, a CAVALIER and five CROSSBOWMEN as the caravan escort: heavy Western European mounted knights and crossbowmen are not what accompanied two Venetian merchants across the Pamirs and Gobi. Camels, Trade Carts and light infantry existed in the engine.
MILITIA and PIKEMEN as the 'Caravan Guards' at a Silk Road trade post: Western European drilled infantry types rather than any steppe or Persian-flavoured unit.
TREE_PALM_FOREST as the dominant vegetation across a route the text describes as 'mountain passes' and the high Pamir/Taklamakan — palms belong to a hot desert oasis, not the Central Asian highlands.

Kublai Khan himself is absent from the scenario despite being the destination and the historically documented host; the 'summer palace at Shangdu' is represented only by a PAVILION_A and two tents plus scattered yurts, not by any Asian-flavoured architecture.
strengths: The Mongol camp is correctly built from YURT_A-D, a GUARD_TOWER and palisade, and garrisoned with six CAVALRY_ARCHERS — a reasonable engine approximation of a steppe encampment.
The escort/waypoint structure with Departure, Midpoint oasis, Enemy Territory, Approaching Goal and Ambush beats does capture the shape of a long overland journey rather than a set-piece battle.

Niccolo Polo is present as a named companion with his own death trigger, correctly reflecting that Marco travelled with his father (and the real journey took years and nearly killed the young Marco through illness).
The market and trade-post episode where local guards join the caravan gestures at the real practice of hiring escorts and joining existing caravans along the route.
justification: The scenario's central figure is RICHARD_THE_LIONHEART, a hero who died in 1199 and never left Europe or the Levant, cast as Marco Polo — a wrong-century, wrong-region substitution the engine did not force, and the bandit chief is a Viking BERSERK. The escort roster of Knights, Cavaliers, Crossbowmen, Militia and Pikemen is a Western European field army rather than a merchant caravan, and the brief's promised pack animals never appear (the only livestock are GAIA sheep). Worse, the narrative makes the Mongols the enemy — 'A Mongol camp guards the mountain pass ahead' and 'the riders of the Khan were waiting in the rocks' — when the historical Polos travelled under Kublai's protection and were received as guests; Kublai Khan himself is not even placed, and Shangdu is a pavilion and two tents. The narrative beats are a generic template (Discover Clue, Betrayal/Twist, Rescue Mission, Villain Speech, Final Battle) with real names pasted on; the historically decisive episodes - Almenar, the capture of Berenguer Ramon II at Tevar, the two-year siege of Valencia in 1093-94, and the defence against Yusuf ibn Tashfin at Cuarte - are absent, replaced by a fortress assault on a fictional 'Saladin's Emir'. But every named leader is a wrong-century substitute: William the Conqueror (1066) plays Charles Martel, Saladin (1180s Levant) plays Abd al-Rahman, and El Cid (1090s Iberia) plays Duke Odo, which is an avoidable choice even within AoE2's limited hero list. A student would retain the correct outcome and a few names from the dialogue while absorbing an essentially medieval, wrong-leader picture of a Renaissance gunpowder siege.

title: The Siege of Vienna
anachronisms_found: SALADIN placed as the Ottoman commander: Saladin was an Ayyubid sultan who died in 1193, roughly 336 years before 1529, and he was never Ottoman. The dialogue calls him 'Enemy Lord'/'the Sultan' while the text names Suleiman, so the placed hero directly contradicts the narration.

Player garrison of MAN_AT_ARMS and CROSSBOWMAN represents 1529 Landsknechts and Spanish arquebusiers; the engine offers Hand Cannoneer (arquebus), Two-Handed Swordsman/Champion and even Landsknecht-analogue Teutonic Knight, so the Feudal-Age roster is an avoidable ~200-year regression with no gunpowder at all on either placed roster.
A generic KING unit stands in for Niklas Graf Salm, a professional soldier and not a monarch; no distinct hero or at least a Teutonic/infantry hero unit was used.
3,083 oak trees blanketing the map turns the Vienna glacis and Danube plain into primeval forest; the historical siege ground was cleared suburbs deliberately burned by the defenders.

No Janissaries, Bombard Cannons or Ottoman camp structures are placed for the besieger, despite the engine's Turkish roster being ideal for 1529; the attacker exists only as trigger spawns of unspecified type.
strengths: The defensive posture is right: the player is the walled garrison behind 156 stone wall segments, four gates and eight guard towers, matching Vienna's medieval curtain wall.
Narration correctly names Suleiman, Commander Salm, the Carinthian Gate as the assault focus, and the autumn rains/supply failure as the reason the Ottomans withdrew.
Wave 3's 'they bring siege weapons' beat gestures at the Ottoman mining and battery against the wall, and the escalating four-wave structure loosely echoes the intensifying assaults of early October.
justification: The text does the historical work — Suleiman, Salm, the Carinthian Gate, the autumn rains — but the placed content contradicts it: the entire Ottoman side consists of one SALADIN hero, a 12th-century Ayyubid sultan standing in for the 1529 Sultan, while the Vienna garrison is Man-at-Arms and Crossbowmen instead of the Landsknechts and arquebusiers the brief promises and that AoE2's Champion/Two-Handed Swordsman and Hand Cannoneer could easily have supplied. Structurally it is a generic four-wave survival map with a 10-minute 'hold until dawn' timer, which misrepresents a three-week siege decided by countermining (entirely absent) and logistics rather than by slaying an enemy commander. A student would learn that Vienna was besieged by 'the Sultan' and held out, but would take away Saladin as the Ottoman leader and a pre-gunpowder picture of a battle fought with arquebuses and cannon.

title: The Rise of Temujin

BOMBARD_CANNON x3 and MANGONEL x2 — gunpowder artillery did not exist on the 12th-century steppe; nothing in Temujin's unification wars involved cannon
CAMEL_RIDER x3 — Middle Eastern/Saracen unit, not a Mongol or Merkit/Naiman formation; the engine's MANGUDAI, cavalry archers and light cavalry were available

57 STONE_WALL segments plus CASTLE, KEEP x2, GUARD_TOWER x3, GATE — European stone fortification for a nomadic steppe confederation that had no stone cities; the player should be a mobile warband, not a walled garrison
KING unit representing the player's leader — Temujin was a steppe khan, and the KING piece encodes a sedentary European monarchy
TREE_PALM_FOREST x10 — palm desert vegetation instead of steppe grassland or Mongolian conifer/birch
CROSSBOWMAN x6, UNIVERSITY, MONASTERY, MARKET — Western European institutional and infantry set entirely alien to the 1186-1206 Mongolian plateau

All 15 triggers and every line of in-game text depict the 1453 Ottoman siege of Constantinople (Constantine XI, Mehmed II, Theodosian Walls, Hagia Sophia, Giustiniani) — a different continent, religion and century from the stated event
strengths: SHEEP x12 and open gold/stone/forage resources at least suggest a pastoral resource economy, though this appears to be incidental map filler rather than intentional steppe design
The trigger chain is internally coherent as a timed siege-defence scenario (probing assault, bombardment, scripted breach, general assault) with functioning defeat conditions
justification: Nothing in this scenario depicts the rise of Temujin: there is no Borte rescue, no Jamukha, no Merkit or Naiman force, and no kurultai — instead all fifteen triggers and every text line narrate the 1453 Ottoman siege of Constantinople, naming Constantine XI, Mehmed II, the Theodosian Walls, the Hagia Sophia and Giustiniani. The placed roster compounds this: the enemy is led by hero SALADIN (d. 1193, Ayyubid Egypt) fielding bombard cannons and camel riders, while the player holds a stone-walled town with a Castle, two Keeps, a University and a Monastery — a fortified European city, the exact opposite of a mobile steppe warband. Palm forest terrain places the map in a desert rather than the Mongolian grassland. A student would learn nothing about Mongol unification and would be actively misinformed, since even the siege that was actually built misattributes its commander.

TREE_PALM_FOREST and desert/oasis terrain - Senlac Hill in Sussex was temperate downland and woodland, not a palm desert

The Anglo-Saxon belligerent is entirely absent, replaced by a steppe raider force of cavalry archers and light cavalry housed in yurts, with Genghis Khan placed as a GAIA hero and El Cid inexplicably in the Norman camp. Terrain is palm-forest desert with an oasis rather than Sussex downland, and there is no shield wall, no feigned retreat, and no Harold. A student would learn nothing about 1066 and would be actively misled about who fought there.

The besieger/besieged roles are inverted, with the enemy holding the walls, castle and gate while the player has a Town Center and Market in the open, and the Ottoman siege train that the engine readily supports (bombard cannon, Janissaries, siege rams) is entirely absent in favour of camel riders and cavalry archers on palm-forest terrain. title: The Battle of Tours
anachronisms_found: WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR hero placed as Player One's leader - William was born c.1028, nearly three centuries after 732; the brief calls for Charles Martel (Charlemagne/Bela/generic hero units were available as substitutes)
KING unit standing in for Harold Godwinson - no king led either side at Tours; Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi was an emir/governor, not a monarch

Player One fielded as KNIGHT x10 with Frankish-style Town Center/Stable/Archery Range - the mounted shock force at Tours was the Umayyad side, and 8th-century Franks fought dismounted with spear and shield, not 11th-century couched-lance knights

No Umayyad/Muslim force at all: Player Two is CHAMPION/SPEARMAN/SKIRMISHER infantry explicitly narrated as a Saxon shield wall, when the historical enemy was Arab-Berber light and heavy cavalry (Camel Rider, Mameluke, or generic light cavalry were all available in the engine)
Only two players exist; the promised third force of Aquitanian allies under Duke Odo is entirely absent
All in-game text is dated 'October 14th, 1066. Near Hastings, England' - wrong century, wrong country, wrong war
strengths: The 2,560 oak trees do create genuinely wooded high ground, which is at least compatible with the forested terrain between Tours and Poitiers
The core tactical idea of infantry holding a ridge against repeated cavalry attacks is thematically adjacent to Tours, even though it is scripted as Hastings
Trigger structure is technically coherent: timed dialogue, an area-based lure/ambush pair, timed reinforcements, and leader-death victory/defeat conditions all fire sensibly
justification: This is not a scenario about Tours at all - it is a complete Hastings 1066 scenario mislabelled, with William the Conqueror placed as the player hero and every line of narration naming Senlac Hill, Harold Godwinson, housecarls and the Norman feigned retreat. Neither historical belligerent appears: there is no Charles Martel, no Abd al-Rahman, no Umayyad cavalry (Player Two is Champion/Spearman infantry), and no third Aquitanian player for Duke Odo despite the brief promising one. The victory condition is 'Slay King Harold before nightfall to win England,' which inverts the actual outcome logic of Tours, where the Frankish defenders repelled an invasion rather than an invader seizing a crown. A student would learn the Battle of Hastings under the wrong name, date, and continent-scale strategic context.

title: The Exile of El Cid
anachronisms_found: WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR is placed as the Player One leader while the text calls him 'Charles Martel' — William (d. 1087) was not at Tours (732), and is also not El Cid's antagonist Alfonso VI

SALADIN is placed as the Muslim commander and named 'Abd al-Rahman' in text — Saladin (1137-1193) postdates both Tours by four centuries and El Cid's exile by a half-century; the engine offers no Iberian Muslim hero, but Saladin plus the Tours labelling is doubly wrong

All in-game text is set in 'October, 732 AD... between Tours and Poitiers', not 1081-1094 Iberia; Duke Odo of Aquitaine and the Umayyad Caliphate are entirely the wrong belligerents for El Cid's exile

EL_CID exists only as a third player's tiny retinue (1 hero, 3 knights, 3 men-at-arms, 3 scouts) with two tents and no role in any trigger — the titular protagonist is absent from every objective, victory, and defeat condition
CAMEL_RIDER x7 for the 'Umayyad' force at Tours — no camel cavalry crossed the Pyrenees in 732, and for an Iberian Taifa scenario Saracen/Berber light cavalry would be the appropriate choice
4,640 TREE_OAK covering the map depicts a wooded northern Gallic ridge, not the arid Ebro valley or Levantine huerta of Zaragoza and Valencia

No Zaragoza, Valencia, or any Muslim-style walled city is built anywhere; Player One uses a TOWN_CENTER, BARRACKS, ARCHERY_RANGE, BLACKSMITH and MONASTERY set with GUARD_TOWERs — a generic European camp, not an Iberian siege objective
strengths: The EL_CID hero unit does exist somewhere on the map, and his retinue is at least composed of period-plausible Castilian types (knights, men-at-arms, scout cavalry)
Gold and stone mines, forage bushes, deer and sheep give a functional resource layout
The Tours narration itself is reasonably well written and quotes the Mozarabic chronicle's 'wall, immovable as a block of ice' line accurately — it is simply attached to the wrong scenario
justification: This is not a scenario about El Cid's exile at all: every line of narration, every objective, and all fourteen triggers depict the Battle of Tours in 732, with Charles Martel, Abd al-Rahman and Duke Odo of Aquitaine as the named actors. The placed heroes contradict even that fiction — WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR stands in for Charles Martel and SALADIN for Abd al-Rahman, both centuries out of period and avoidable given the engine's hero list. El Cid himself is a decorative third party with three knights and two tents, referenced in no trigger, so the stated loss condition ('losing El Cid himself means defeat') is instead scripted as 'Charles Martel Killed'; worse, both defeat triggers call DECLARE_VICTORY. A student would learn nothing about Zaragoza, Alfonso VI, or the 1094 conquest of Valencia, and would come away with a garbled account of Tours as well.

Player roster of ARCHER, MAN_AT_ARMS, PIKEMAN, KNIGHT contains no gunpowder units at all, though the brief promises German Landsknechts (Two-Handed Swordsman) and Spanish arquebusiers (Hand Cannoneer), both available in the engine
PAVILION_A/TENT_A and FLAG_A placed as the player's camp - the player in 1529 is a walled-city garrison, not a field encampment
ROMAN_RUINS and open forest map with 640 oak trees and deer/sheep: an open-field march map, not the fortified city of Vienna with its medieval curtain wall, bastions and the Carinthian Gate

Two walled towns with CASTLE, GATE and STONE_WALL are constructed and garrisoned, so siege-of-a-fortified-place mechanics exist in the file even though they belong to the wrong campaign
justification: This is not a Siege of Vienna scenario at all: every placed object and every line of text depicts Joan of Arc's June 1429 escort of the Dauphin Charles through English-held Champagne to his coronation at Reims. The objectives invert the historical situation entirely, turning a defensive hold-until-the-autumn-rains siege into an offensive escort march. anachronisms_found: RICHARD_THE_LIONHEART placed as the player's hero — a late 12th-century English king, not Charles Martel (732); the engine offers Charlemagne/Frankish-flavoured heroes and generic infantry, so this was avoidable

CAMEL_RIDER x4 and CAVALRY_ARCHER/LIGHT_CAVALRY as the opposing force — steppe/Mongol cavalry idiom, not Umayyad heavy horse in the Loire valley; the engine's Knight/Camel choice aside, camels in Touraine are absurd
YURT_A/B/C/D x6 as the enemy camp architecture — Central Asian nomad dwellings standing in for an Umayyad camp in Gaul
TREE_PALM_FOREST x18 covering the map — the brief specifies wooded high ground between Tours and Poitiers; palms belong to a desert/oasis map
PIKEMAN x6 — a 14th–15th-century unit type; Frankish 732 infantry should be Militia/Spearman-class
BERSERK — a Norse unit, out of place for a Frankish or Aquitanian contingent in 732

justification: The built scenario is not the Battle of Tours in any respect: every line of narration describes Marco Polo's 1271 journey from Venice to Shangdu, the hero unit is Richard the Lionheart, the enemy is a Mongol camp of six yurts defended by camel riders and cavalry archers, and the map is a palm-forest desert rather than wooded Loire-valley high ground. The victory condition is 'bring object to area' (reach Shangdu) with an escort-and-ambush beat sequence, the exact opposite of a defensive stand that repels cavalry charges; Charles Martel, Abd al-Rahman and Duke Odo appear nowhere in the placed content. A student would learn about a garbled Silk Road expedition, not the 732 Umayyad invasion of Gaul.

title: The Exile of El Cid
anachronisms_found: WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR is the player's hero: the wrong man, wrong country, wrong decade (Normandy 1066, not Castile/Zaragoza/Valencia 1081-1094). The engine offers El Cid himself as a hero unit, so this was entirely avoidable.

Player TWO's roster of CHAMPION, SPEARMAN and SKIRMISHER behind STONE_WALL and GUARD_TOWERs represents a Saxon shield wall, not the Muslim taifa armies of Zaragoza, Lerida, Valencia or the Almoravids; no Saracen/camel/light-cavalry or Middle-Eastern-architecture elements appear anywhere.

A generic KING unit stands in for Harold Godwinson; the actual antagonists of the exile (al-Musta'in of Zaragoza's rivals, Berenguer Ramon II of Barcelona, al-Qadir/Ibn Jahhaf of Valencia, Yusuf ibn Tashfin) are absent entirely.
Map is 4,174 oak trees - a north-European woodland, not the arid Ebro valley or Levantine huerta of Valencia.
ROMAN_RUINS and a lone SKELETON are the only 'flavour' objects; no Iberian city, no walled Valencia to besiege despite the brief naming its conquest as the climax.
All dialogue references Senlac Hill, October 14th 1066, housecarls, fyrd levies and Norman feigned retreats - fifteen years before the scenario's stated start date and 1,500 km away.
strengths: The scenario is technically competent on its own terms: hero-death defeat condition, timed narration, patrol and reinforcement triggers, and difficulty-scaling triggers all function.
The 'keep the hero alive or lose' logic would have suited the El Cid brief, had the hero been El Cid.
justification: This is not a scenario about El Cid's exile at all: it is a Battle of Hastings scenario, with WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR as the player's hero, a generic KING standing in for Harold, and sixteen lines of narration explicitly dated 'October 14th, 1066' on 'Senlac Hill'. Nothing in the placed content touches Iberia - no El Cid hero (which the engine provides), no Muslim taifa forces, no Zaragoza or Valencia, and a 4,174-oak north-European forest map instead of the Ebro or Levante. The objectives ('Break the Saxon shield wall. Slay King Harold') bear no relation to the mercenary-service arc described in the brief. A student would come away believing El Cid's exile was the Norman conquest of England.

title: The Road to Reims
anachronisms_found: EL_CID hero placed as the player character - Rodrigo Diaz de Vivar died in 1099, 330 years before the 1429 march to Reims; Joan of Arc (JOAN_OF_ARC) and Charles VII (CHARLES_DE_LA_TOUR / the Dauphin) exist in the engine and were avoidable omissions

ROMAN_RUINS and TEMPLE_RUIN decorations evoking a Levantine/Iberian setting rather than French towns and Reims cathedral (a Monastery or Wonder could have stood in for the cathedral)
